page_title: Write tests. Not too many. Mostly integration.

sources.entry: Write tests. Not too many. Mostly integration. for a contrarian take about unit testing

summary.title: Write tests. Not too many. Mostly integration.
summary.one_liner: Learn why Kent C. Dodds argues for fewer, mostly integration-level tests over 100% coverage and heavy unit-test mocking, using his Testing Trophy model.
takeaways: Aim for confidence that the app works, not for a coverage number; the author says returns diminish well before 100% coverage.
Use static typing and linting (TypeScript, ESLint) for cheap checks, but still write tests for business logic.
Spend most testing effort on integration tests, which give a good balance of confidence and speed compared with unit and E2E tests.
Reduce mocking to increase integration confidence, and avoid testing implementation details so refactoring does not break tests.
summary.summary: Kent C. Dodds expands on Guillermo Rauch's tweet, "Write tests. Not too many. Mostly integration.", section by section. He argues for automated tests, warns against mandating 100% coverage and testing implementation details, and says static typing and linting cover some bugs but not business logic. He presents the testing pyramid and his own Testing Trophy, noting that higher-level tests bring more confidence despite being slower. He closes with advice to write more integration tests by mocking less, including avoiding shallow rendering in React.
